name: Sinding-Larsen–Johansson syndrome
summary: A traction apophysitis at the inferior pole of the patella in active adolescents. It causes activity-related pain at the lower kneecap and usually settles with load modification, though the evidence is limited.

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Uncommon: about 0.8% of 12–15-year-olds had MRI features in one cohort; quoted rates of 2–5% come from a case report

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mainly physically active adolescents aged 9–17 years, more often boys

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Focal tenderness at the inferior pole of the patella with a normal straight-leg raise; no validated test accuracy data

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs may be normal early; ultrasound or MRI is the most useful. Exclude patellar sleeve fracture

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Conservative care reported to give positive outcomes within about 2–8 months; evidence is mostly case reports

keyFacts.label: Management
keyFacts.value: Education, load management and progressive exercise (extrapolated from Osgood–Schlatter disease)

overview:
Sinding-Larsen–Johansson syndrome (SLJ) is an osteochondrosis of the inferior pole of the patella. In the original prospective description, it was a traction tendinitis with de novo calcification at the proximal attachment of the patellar tendon, which had been partially avulsed. The course was self-limited and benign, like that of Osgood–Schlatter disease [r1]. Together with Osgood–Schlatter disease it is one of the forms of knee apophysitis seen in young athletes [r2].

It mainly affects physically active adolescents aged 9–17 years, especially boys, and presents as localised knee pain [r3]. Its clinical presentation does not differ much from Osgood–Schlatter disease, so imaging helps to make the diagnosis [r4]. The main diagnostic hazard is a patellar sleeve fracture, which can look similar on radiographs but is managed very differently [r5].

The evidence base is thin. A 2024 scoping review found that the literature on SLJ is mainly case studies and is limited and often conflicting [r3]. There are no trials of treatment. Management therefore rests on conservative principles shared with other traction apophysitis conditions, and on the pain-monitored load management and strengthening used for Osgood–Schlatter disease [r6,r3].

epidemiology.text: SLJ is uncommon. A population-based MRI study of 1910 adolescents aged 12–15 years found features of SLJ in 16 (0.8%), compared with 43 (2.3%) for Osgood–Schlatter disease [r7]. A case report quotes an incidence of 2–5% in children aged 10–15 years, but that figure is secondhand and its source was not checked [r8]. The scoping review describes SLJ as affecting physically active adolescents aged 9–17 years, particularly males [r3]. In a series of 125 skeletally immature patients with SLJ or other inferior pole pathologies, 82% were male, the mean age was 10.7 years, and patient characteristics did not differ between the diagnoses [r5]. Reliable population incidence by age and sex was not identified.

intrinsic: Skeletal immaturity: the condition occurs in growing children and adolescents, mainly 9–17 years [r3]
Male sex (more affected in the scoping review and in a paediatric inferior pole series) [r3,r5]
Quadriceps tightness and growth-spurt effects, extrapolated from Osgood–Schlatter disease and not confirmed for SLJ [r9]
A history of other traction apophysitis, such as Osgood–Schlatter disease, is plausible but not quantified for SLJ [r2]
extrinsic: Sports involving repeated jumping and running, such as basketball, volleyball, soccer and gymnastics [r8,r3]
High training volume and intensity during growth (common clinical observation; not quantified in the sources reviewed)
Repeated microtrauma to the inferior pole of the patella is the proposed cause [r10,r1]

mechanism.summary: SLJ is a traction injury. Repeated quadriceps contraction in jumping, running and kicking pulls the patella proximally, and the patellar tendon holds the inferior pole of the patella. The tendon attachment on the growing inferior pole is the weak link, so the tendon is loaded at its proximal attachment, which can be partially avulsed, with de novo calcification [r1]. The condition is attributed to repeated microtrauma [r10]. It usually lacks a single injury event, although an acute presentation after a non-contact jump or kick has been reported [r11,r5].
sequence: A physically active child or adolescent trains with repeated jumping, running and kicking [r3,r8].
Each quadriceps contraction pulls the patella upward, and the patellar tendon resists at the inferior pole of the patella.
The inferior pole is a growing site of attachment that is relatively weak, so repeated tensile loading causes microtrauma at the proximal tendon attachment [r10,r1].
The tendon attachment may be partially avulsed, and calcification can appear in the proximal tendon [r1].
Pain and local tenderness develop at the inferior pole, and an ossicle or small fragment can appear on imaging [r3,r11].
Symptoms settle in most cases with reduced loading and time, and the condition was reported to be self-limited [r1,r3].

variants.name: Chronic overuse (typical)
variants.description: Gradual onset anterior knee pain at the inferior pole of the patella with sport. A small minority recall an injury [r5].

variants.name: Acute presentation
variants.description: A sudden pain after a non-contact soccer injury in a 10-year-old, with swelling and a minimally displaced distal patellar ossicle. MRI excluded a sleeve injury and confirmed SLJ, and the knee healed in 4 weeks after brief immobilisation [r11]. This is a single case report.

variants.name: Overlap with patellar sleeve avulsion fracture
variants.description: A 12-year-old with SLJ later sustained an inferior pole sleeve avulsion fracture during a high jump. Whether SLJ increases the risk of sleeve fracture is not clear [r12]. A minimally displaced sleeve fracture was also reported in a child with bilateral SLJ [r5].

variants.name: Persistent SLJ in a skeletally mature athlete
variants.description: Painful SLJ lesion in a 29-year-old professional handball player that persisted after 4 months of eccentric rehabilitation and platelet-rich plasma injections. Arthroscopic excision relieved symptoms [r10]. This is a single case report.

anatomy.text: The patella is a sesamoid bone in the quadriceps and patellar tendon. The patellar tendon runs from the inferior pole of the patella to the tibial tuberosity. In children the inferior pole is a growing site of tendon attachment, and the proximal patellar tendon attaches there with fibrocartilage. The infrapatellar fat pad lies behind the proximal tendon, and the deep infrapatellar bursa lies beneath the distal tendon.

structures.name: Inferior pole of the patella
structures.role: Growing attachment site of the proximal patellar tendon; the site of SLJ [r1,r10]

structures.name: Proximal patellar tendon
structures.role: Transmits quadriceps force from the patella to the tibia. In SLJ it is partially avulsed with calcification at its proximal attachment [r1].

structures.name: Quadriceps and quadriceps tendon
structures.role: Knee extensors that pull the patella proximally; repeated contraction produces the traction load

structures.name: Infrapatellar fat pad
structures.role: Cushion behind the proximal tendon, which may be irritated in adjacent anterior knee pain conditions

structures.name: Tibial tuberosity apophysis
structures.role: The distal end of the same extensor mechanism and the site of Osgood–Schlatter disease [r2]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Pathology in SLJ is repeated traction at the proximal patellar tendon attachment on the inferior pole of the patella. In the original prospective study of eight patients (ten knees), the cause appeared to be a traction tendinitis with de novo calcification in the proximal attachment of the patellar tendon, which had been partially avulsed [r1]. A 2024 scoping review described SLJ as mainly affecting active adolescents with localised knee pain. Ultrasound and MRI were the most effective diagnostic tools [r3]. Radiographs may show no significant changes in the acute setting [r8], but a distal patellar ossicle can be seen [r11].

The disorder is best understood as load exceeding the capacity of a growing attachment. Most youth overuse injuries occur at the epiphyses and apophyses, which are relatively weak [r2]. Apart from the original case series, the sources reviewed contained no histology or cellular studies of SLJ, so the cellular timeline below is a schematic model drawn from the traction description. The evidence is limited and often conflicting [r3].

structures.name: Inferior pole of the patella
structures.effect: Traction stress, with a small bony fragment or ossicle on imaging in some cases [r1,r11]

structures.name: Proximal patellar tendon attachment
structures.effect: Partial avulsion with de novo calcification in the original description [r1]

structures.name: Overlying soft tissue
structures.effect: Localised swelling and tenderness. Knee effusion was uncommon (3% in a paediatric inferior pole series) [r5].

structures.name: Patellar sleeve
structures.effect: Can be avulsed in a related fracture that mimics SLJ. A sleeve avulsion fracture is a different injury, and treatment of it is frequently surgical [r13,r12].

muscles.name: Quadriceps
muscles.effect: Repeated forceful contraction produces the traction load. Tightness and weakness were linked with Osgood–Schlatter disease and may be relevant here [r9].

muscles.name: Hamstrings
muscles.effect: Reduced flexibility is a proposed contributor in the related condition [r9]

muscles.name: Hip and trunk muscles
muscles.effect: Control of landing and jumping mechanics, which affects the load at the extensor mechanism (clinical reasoning; no SLJ data)

cellular.timing: Weeks to months of repeated loading
cellular.description: Repeated tensile loading of the patellar attachment causes microtrauma [r10,r1]. This is inferred from the traction description.
Pain and local irritation. A partial avulsion at the proximal tendon attachment with de novo calcification was seen in the original study [r1].
A small bony fragment may be seen at the distal pole of the patella [r11].
Conservative treatment reportedly gave positive outcomes within 2–8 months [r3]. The disease was described as self-limited and benign [r1], but a small number persist into adulthood [r10].

systems.effect: Rapid growth increases demand on the extensor mechanism while the attachment is still a growth site [r2,r3].
Pain is local and load-related at first. Long-term pain data for SLJ were not identified.
Quadriceps and hamstring flexibility, and hip and trunk control during landing, affect extensor loading (extrapolated from Osgood–Schlatter disease) [r9].
Sport participation may be restricted for months [r3]. Adolescents with Osgood–Schlatter disease report lower quality of life despite high activity levels, but this has not been studied in SLJ [r14].
SLJ can coexist with, or be mistaken for, a patellar sleeve fracture, which can be missed on plain radiographs [r5,r12].

timeframes.summary: Evidence is limited to case reports. A 2024 scoping review found that conservative treatment, mainly activity limitation, yielded positive outcomes within about 2–8 months [r3]. The original study reported a self-limited, benign course [r1]. One acute case healed within 4 weeks after brief immobilisation [r11]. No tissue-healing data specific to SLJ were identified, so the phases below are typical clinical ranges.

healing.description: Reduce provoking jumping, running and kicking, and begin isometric exercise [r3]
Sport is reintroduced in steps; positive outcomes within 2–8 months in case reports [r3]
Most settle with skeletal maturity; some may persist [r1,r10]

milestones.label: Return to full sport
milestones.note: Within the 2–8 month range reported in case studies [r3]

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based. Case studies report positive outcomes within about 2–8 months of conservative care [r3]. There are no validated criteria for SLJ.

symptoms: Localised anterior knee pain at the lower pole of the patella, worse with sport, jumping, kneeling and stairs [r3]
Pain that settles with rest and recurs when activity resumes
Swelling or tenderness at the bottom of the patella, but little knee effusion
Usually gradual onset without a clear injury (only 24% reported acute trauma in one SLJ group) [r5]
Able to walk and bear weight (88% in one SLJ group) [r5]
signs: Focal tenderness at the inferior pole of the patella, at the patellar tendon origin
Pain on resisted knee extension and a single-leg squat or hop
Straight-leg raise intact (98% in one SLJ group, compared with 38% in sleeve fractures) [r5]
Knee swelling present in 41% and effusion in 3% in one SLJ group, compared with 93% and 81% in sleeve fractures [r5]
Normal patellar height and stable patellar tracking

subjective: Age, growth stage, and sports load: jumping, running and kicking volume and any recent increase
Pain location (inferior pole), onset, behaviour with sport and kneeling, and night pain (should be absent)
Mechanism: gradual overuse or an acute jump or kick event (consider sleeve fracture) [r5,r11]
Ability to weight-bear and to lift the straight leg after the event [r5]
Previous treatment, duration and impact on sport and school
Features of other pathology: locking, effusion, fever, night pain, systemic illness
observation: Swelling or a lump at the inferior pole of the patella, compared with the other side
Patellar position: a high or displaced patella suggests sleeve fracture [r5]
palpation: Inferior pole of the patella: focal tenderness (compare with the tibial tuberosity in Osgood–Schlatter disease) [r4]
Proximal patellar tendon and fat pad
Tibial tuberosity, to exclude a combined presentation
rangeOfMotion: Knee flexion and extension are usually full
Rectus femoris and hamstring flexibility (extrapolated from Osgood–Schlatter disease) [r9]
Hip range of motion to screen for referred pain
strength: Active straight-leg raise: preserved in SLJ and often lost in sleeve fractures [r5]
Knee extension strength by hand-held dynamometry, compared with the other side
functional: Single-leg squat or step-down with pain recorded
Jump and hop tests when pain allows

specialTests.name: Palpation of the inferior pole of the patella
specialTests.purpose: Locate the pain source and separate SLJ from Osgood–Schlatter disease
specialTests.procedure: With the knee extended and the quadriceps relaxed, palpate the lower pole of the patella and the proximal tendon origin. Palpate the tibial tuberosity for comparison.
specialTests.positive: Focal tenderness at the inferior pole. No diagnostic accuracy data were identified in the sources reviewed.

specialTests.name: Active straight-leg raise
specialTests.purpose: Screen for extensor mechanism disruption and patellar sleeve fracture
specialTests.procedure: Patient supine. Ask the patient to lift the straight leg against gravity with the knee locked.
specialTests.positive: An inability to lift the leg, or an extensor lag, suggests sleeve fracture rather than SLJ (the raise was intact in 38% of sleeve fractures and 98% of SLJ patients in one series) [r5].

specialTests.name: Resisted knee extension
specialTests.purpose: Reproduce traction pain at the patellar attachment
specialTests.procedure: Patient seated with the knee flexed to about 90°. The patient extends the knee against resistance while the examiner palpates the inferior pole.
specialTests.positive: Familiar pain at the inferior pole. No accuracy data were identified.

specialTests.name: Single-leg squat or hop
specialTests.procedure: Single-leg squat to about 45–60° or a single-leg hop, recording pain and control.
specialTests.positive: Pain at the inferior pole or poor control. No accuracy data were identified.

outcomeMeasures.name: Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) subscales
outcomeMeasures.use: Pain, sport and recreation and quality of life; used in OSD cohorts and suitable for adolescents [r6]

outcomeMeasures.name: Numeric pain rating during and 24 hours after sport
Global rating of change
outcomeMeasures.use: Used as the primary outcome in an OSD case series [r6]

imaging.indication: Atypical or acute presentation, trauma, or inability to straight-leg raise
imaging.findings: May be normal in the acute setting [r8]. A distal patellar ossicle or small fragment may be seen [r11]. Patellar height is normal in SLJ, compared with patella alta in sleeve fractures [r5].

imaging.indication: Diagnostic doubt in a child with localised inferior pole pain
imaging.findings: Ultrasound and MRI are the most effective diagnostic tools in the scoping review [r3]. Ultrasound has been described as the modality of choice when radiographs are normal [r8].

imaging.indication: Suspected sleeve fracture or when the diagnosis is uncertain after radiographs
imaging.findings: Excludes sleeve cartilaginous injury and shows the apophyseal traction injury [r11]. MRI features of SLJ were found in 0.8% of a general adolescent population, so correlate with symptoms [r7].

differentials.name: Patellar sleeve avulsion fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Acute trauma in 100% of cases, effusion in 81%, an inability to straight-leg raise in most, and patella alta with a displaced fragment [r5]. It needs urgent imaging and orthopaedic referral.

differentials.name: Osgood–Schlatter disease
differentials.distinguishing: Tenderness at the tibial tuberosity rather than the inferior pole of the patella. The clinical presentation is similar [r4,r2].

differentials.name: Patellar tendinopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Occurs mostly in skeletally mature jumping athletes, with pain in the proximal tendon rather than the apophysis

differentials.name: Patellofemoral pain
differentials.distinguishing: Diffuse peripatellar pain with stairs, squatting and sitting, and no focal tenderness at the inferior pole

differentials.name: Hoffa fat pad impingement
differentials.distinguishing: Pain beside the patellar tendon with extension and standing, and a tender fat pad

differentials.name: Bipartite patella or other normal variant
differentials.distinguishing: A normal variant that may be found on imaging in 1.1% of adolescents and mistaken for a fracture or apophysitis. Match imaging to symptoms [r7].

differentials.name: Osteochondritis dissecans of the knee
differentials.distinguishing: Deeper pain, effusion or mechanical symptoms, and a lesion on imaging

redFlags: Acute pain after a jump, kick or fall with an inability to straight-leg raise, a high-riding or displaced patella, a large effusion or an inability to bear weight: suspect a patellar sleeve avulsion fracture. Arrange urgent radiographs or MRI and orthopaedic referral [r5,r12].
A fragment that is displaced on imaging or a palpable gap: refer for surgical opinion [r5].
Night pain, constant pain unrelated to activity, fever or an enlarging firm mass: suspect infection or a bone tumour. Arrange blood tests and imaging, and refer.
A hot, red, swollen knee with fever or the patient unwell: suspect septic arthritis. Refer to the emergency department.
A limp or reduced hip movement with knee pain: examine the hip and refer for hip pathology such as slipped capital femoral epiphysis.
Failure to improve after about 3 months of well-delivered care, or pain persisting after skeletal maturity: arrange imaging review and consider surgical opinion [r10].

management.principles: The evidence for SLJ management is limited to case reports and a scoping review, which concluded that the literature is mainly case studies and is limited and often conflicting [r3]. There are no trials of treatment. Management follows the principles of other traction apophysitis conditions: education, reduced provocative loading rather than complete rest, and progressive strengthening, using the pain-monitored program developed for Osgood–Schlatter disease as the best available template [r6]. That program is itself a small uncontrolled case series. The scoping review recommended conservative care with rest or cryotherapy, passive mobilisation, isometric exercise and NSAIDs, reporting positive outcomes within 2–8 months [r3]. Always exclude a patellar sleeve avulsion fracture first [r5]. Surgery is rarely considered [r10].

medical.name: Short-term analgesia (paracetamol or a brief NSAID course)
medical.description: For pain flare-ups, while load is modified. NSAIDs were among the measures recommended by the scoping review's authors [r3].

medical.name: Brief immobilisation or protected weight-bearing
medical.description: Used for 4 weeks in a single acute case with a minimally displaced ossicle while a sleeve fracture was excluded [r11]. Not needed for typical overuse presentations.

medical.name: Arthroscopic excision of the symptomatic lesion
medical.description: Reserved for persistent painful SLJ in the skeletally mature after failed conservative care. A 29-year-old professional handball player returned to competitive sport 5 months after excision [r10]. Single case report.

medical.name: Surgical fixation for a patellar sleeve avulsion fracture
medical.description: Not SLJ. A displaced sleeve avulsion fracture, including one in a child with prior SLJ, was fixed with transosseous tapes and gave good results [r12]. Differentiating this from SLJ is important because treatment of sleeve fractures is frequently surgical [r13].

physio.name: Education and pain-monitored load management
physio.description: Explain the condition, agree a pain limit, and reduce jumping, sprinting and kicking volume to stay within it, rather than stopping sport. The scoping review reported that activity limitation gave positive outcomes in 2–8 months [r3]. The pain-monitored approach is extrapolated from the OSD case series [r6].

physio.name: Isometric then progressive strengthening
physio.description: Isometric exercise was recommended in the scoping review [r3]. Progression to knee, hip and calf strengthening follows the OSD program, in which knee extension strength rose by 32% and hip abduction by 24% at 12 weeks [r6]. This has not been tested in SLJ.

physio.name: Cryotherapy and passive mobilisation
physio.description: Recommended by the scoping review's authors for symptom relief [r3]. They do not change the course.

physio.name: Quadriceps and hamstring stretching
physio.description: Suggested for Osgood–Schlatter disease, with apparent efficacy but no RCT [r15,r9]. Extrapolated to SLJ.

physio.name: Prolonged immobilisation or complete rest as the only treatment
physio.description: No SLJ study supports it. Complete cessation was not required in the OSD case series, which kept adolescents active within a pain limit [r6]. The acute case needing brief immobilisation was a special situation [r11].

education: SLJ is an overuse problem of the growth area at the bottom of the kneecap. It is not a problem of the knee joint itself, and it usually settles as growth finishes [r1,r3].
You usually do not have to stop all sport. Keep pain within an agreed limit during and after activity, and cut back jumping, sprinting and kicking if it goes beyond that.
Strong thighs, hips and calves help the knee cope with the pulling forces of sport, so exercises are an important part of recovery.
Recovery may take several months [r3], so progress is gradual.
See a doctor urgently if you have sudden severe pain after a jump or kick, cannot lift your straight leg or walk, or if there is swelling, a limp, night pain or fever [r5].

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based and follows load versus capacity: settle symptoms by reducing the load that exceeds what the inferior pole currently tolerates, build capacity with isometric then progressive strengthening, add jumping and running in steps, then return to sport. The program is adapted from the Osgood–Schlatter disease case series and the scoping review of SLJ, because no SLJ-specific protocol exists [r6,r3]. Dosages are typical clinical ranges, not drawn from a single trial. As a working rule, activity pain should stay at or below about 3/10 and settle within 24 hours (clinical convention). Check at each review for sleeve fracture features such as loss of straight-leg raise [r5].

stages.name: Settle & plan the load
goals: Explain SLJ and agree a pain limit
Reduce load that provokes pain above the limit
Maintain fitness and sport participation where pain allows
precautions: Avoid repeated jumping and sprinting that provoke pain above the limit (clinical convention)
Avoid direct pressure on the inferior pole
Refer if the straight-leg raise is lost, or after an acute pop [r5]

exercises.name: Isometric wall sit
exercises.dosage: 5 × 30–45 s, daily, at a pain-free depth (about 60° of knee flexion)
exercises.cues: Weight through the heels; knees over the toes

exercises.name: Quadriceps set
exercises.cues: Push the back of the knee down; tighten the thigh

exercises.name: Glute bridge
exercises.cues: Drive through the heels; keep the pelvis level

progressionCriteria: Daily activity pain at or below 3/10
Wall sit 5 × 30 s without increased pain the next day
Straight-leg raise intact with no lag
Understands the pain limit and load plan

stages.name: Build capacity
goals: Increase knee extensor and hip strength
Keep activity pain within the limit
precautions: Keep pain at or below about 3/10 and settled within 24 hours (clinical convention)
Avoid heavy open-chain knee extension if it provokes inferior pole pain

exercises.name: Squat to a box
exercises.cues: Knees over toes; weight through the whole foot

exercises.name: Step-up
exercises.cues: Pelvis level; knee tracks over the second toe

exercises.name: Split squat
exercises.cues: Upright trunk; front knee over the foot

exercises.name: Romanian deadlift
exercises.cues: Hinge at the hip with a long spine

progressionCriteria: Squat and step-up pain at or below 3/10
Single-leg squat to 45–60° with good control
No increase in inferior pole pain the next morning

stages.name: Power & jump readiness
goals: Knee extension strength close to the other side
Reintroduce jumping and landing in small doses
precautions: Increase jumping and sprint volume in small steps
Stop the session if pain exceeds the limit

exercises.name: Jump-squat and soft landing
exercises.cues: Land quietly on bent hips and knees

exercises.name: Walk–run intervals
exercises.dosage: e.g. 1 min run / 1 min walk × 10, then progress as symptoms allow (clinical convention)

progressionCriteria: Activity pain at or below 3/10, settled within 24 hours
Knee extension strength about 90% of the other side (clinical convention)

stages.name: Graded return to sport
goals: Return to full training and match play
precautions: Increase sport-specific volume in steps, for example 10–20% a week (clinical convention)
Review the plan after higher-load weeks or a growth spurt
Reassess for sleeve fracture signs after any acute pop or fall

exercises.name: Sport-specific drills at progressive volume
exercises.dosage: Increase jumping, sprinting or kicking in steps, with at least one lower-load day between
exercises.cues: Keep pain at or below the agreed limit

exercises.name: Planned then unplanned cutting and landing drills
Heavy strength maintenance (squat, split squat, hamstrings)
Stretching and mobility routine
exercises.dosage: 2–3 times a week, 30 s per stretch

progressionCriteria: Full training with pain at or below 3/10 and settling within 24 hours
No inferior pole pain after matches
Strength and jump performance close to the other side

criteria: No validated SLJ-specific return-to-sport (RTS) criteria were identified in the sources reviewed. The criteria below reflect clinical convention.
Pain during and after sport at or below the agreed limit (about 3/10) and settling within 24 hours
No tenderness at the inferior pole after loading, and a full pain-free range of motion
Knee extension and hip strength about 90% of the other side
Jump and landing tasks without pain or knee collapse
A graded plan for sport volume, with a review point after each increase
tests: Hand-held dynamometry of knee extension and hip abduction
Pain monitoring (numeric rating scale) during and 24 hours after sport

prognosis: The original prospective study found the course to be self-limited and benign, like Osgood–Schlatter disease [r1]. The 2024 scoping review found that conservative treatment, mainly activity limitation, gave positive outcomes within two to eight months, but this evidence comes from case studies and is limited and often conflicting [r3]. An acute case with a minimally displaced ossicle healed within 4 weeks after brief immobilisation [r11]. A small number of cases persist, including a 29-year-old athlete whose painful lesion needed arthroscopic excision [r10]. No long-term cohort follow-up of SLJ was identified. Osgood–Schlatter disease, which is similar, had persistent pain in 60.5% of responders at a median of 3.75 years in a retrospective study, so reassurance about complete resolution should be cautious [r16].
prevention: No prevention strategy for SLJ has been tested in the sources reviewed.
Match jumping, running and kicking volume to growth stage, and increase load gradually (clinical opinion; no trial data identified).
Quadriceps and hamstring stretching is suggested for the related Osgood–Schlatter disease, with limited evidence [r9,r15].
Include strength and landing-control training in youth sport programs, and act early on inferior pole pain by modifying load.
clinicalPearls: Always exclude a patellar sleeve avulsion fracture. An intact straight-leg raise, normal patellar height, ability to bear weight and little effusion favour SLJ [r5].
SLJ and Osgood–Schlatter disease look alike. Palpate both the inferior pole of the patella and the tibial tuberosity [r4].
Radiographs can be normal early. If the picture is unclear, use ultrasound or MRI [r3,r8].
SLJ features appear on MRI in about 0.8% of a general adolescent population, so match any imaging finding to the symptoms [r7].
Be honest about the evidence: SLJ treatment advice is largely drawn from case reports and from Osgood–Schlatter disease [r3,r6].
A child with SLJ who has an acute pop after a jump needs reassessment for sleeve fracture, because the two have been reported together [r12].

captions.text: An active 12-year-old volleyball player trains and jumps many times a week.
Each jump loads the quadriceps, which pulls the patella upward.
On landing the patellar tendon holds the lower pole of the patella against that pull.
In a growing child that attachment is still a growth site and is relatively weak.
When load builds faster than the attachment can adapt, load exceeds capacity.
There is usually no single injury: pain builds at the bottom of the kneecap over weeks.
Zooming into the right knee from the side.

actions.text: Patellar tendon: attaches to the inferior pole

captions.text: The patellar tendon attaches to the inferior pole of the patella, a growing site in children.
The quadriceps pulls the patella up while the tendon holds the lower pole: this is traction.
At rest the tendon relaxes. With each jump or kick it is loaded again.
Repeated pulling stresses the inferior pole of the patella, the weak link in the growing skeleton.
In the original description the proximal tendon attachment was partially avulsed, with calcification.
Pain and tenderness appear at the lower pole of the patella, and a small ossicle may show on imaging.
Most cases settle with load management, but the evidence is limited to case reports.
Healthy growth cartilage at the tendon attachment: orderly cells that lay down new bone.
Repeated tendon pull loads the cartilage in tension, which it is poor at resisting.
Load exceeds capacity: microdamage appears at the cartilage–bone junction.
Local irritation develops, and the area becomes sensitive and painful.
A small fragment may separate. This is a schematic model; SLJ-specific tissue data are lacking.
With load management and graded strength work, the area settles over months as growth proceeds.
